Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I feel isolated and set apart from others

issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma in a 34-year-old Navy Officer, 'Known People: Related people' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger without any accompanying memory or appraisal content about bereavement, loss of specific others, or interpersonal aspects of the disaster. The rest of the profile does not explain why related people would be a salient trigger.

issues.item: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Evaluation' is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. It suggests social/performance shame concerns, but the negative appraisals and memory items do not involve appearance, performance failure, humiliation, or social judgment. This maladaptive strategy appears to address a symptom theme not otherwise represented.

'Avoid Friends' similarly implies socially driven withdrawal, yet the selected appraisals are global despair and alienation rather than fear of specific interpersonal consequences, and the trigger set does not include friendship or social contact themes. It is not impossible, but in combination with 'Avoid Evaluation' it pulls toward a social-evaluative formulation not supported elsewhere.

For a natural-disaster trauma in a Navy officer, 'Similar cars' is hard to connect clinically to the rest of the profile. The other triggers are generic situational reminders (crowding, locations), but this item implies a specific vehicle-related cue that is not supported by the trauma type, memory content, or appraisals.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals are extremely global and severe ('life not worth living', 'belong nowhere') relative to the rest of the selected items, which focus on trauma reminders, fragmented imagery, and avoidance. This creates a coherence problem because the profile lacks corresponding threat content or broader self-concept material to support such pervasive suicidal/existential beliefs.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'I no longer belong anywhere' is especially difficult to reconcile with the demographic/contextual profile of a married Navy officer after a natural disaster unless other items indicate moral injury, social alienation, or occupational rupture; none are present in the selected components.

vignette: The storm had hit the coastal naval base with terrifying speed, turning familiar concrete corridors into rising channels of black water. Elias Vance, a thirty-four-year-old Navy Officer, had been trapped on the third-level command deck when the surge breached the bulkheads. What frightened him most was the sudden collapse of order: the deafening roar of wind, the frantic press of men shoulder-to-shoulder in the narrow escape stairwells, and the way the rising water swallowed the emergency lights, plunging everything into absolute darkness. He had been pinned against a railing, his body locked in the exact posture he had held for hours while waiting for rescue, while his mind replayed the disaster as a series of stark, unblinking photographs. Even now, months later, the memory retains such extreme visual clarity that he sometimes struggles to believe it actually happened to him, as if the event were a film rather than a lived catastrophe. When Elias steps onto the base today, the cognitive cycle begins almost immediately. Navigating the crowded briefing rooms or walking past the old waterfront docks acts as a potent trigger, pulling those stark visual memories and bodily reenactments directly into his present awareness. The mere scent of alcohol wafting from the mess hall storage or the press of a crowded deck settles into a quiet certainty that he has lost his happiness entirely and no longer belongs anywhere. This sudden surge of physical and visual recall does not stay isolated; it directly fuels his avoidance. He stops seeing his friends, cancels weekend gatherings, and refuses to enter dimly lit hangars or darkened corridors. The sheer intensity of the reenactment makes him believe he deserves to suffer for surviving when others did not, pushing him to construct punishments and retreat from the world. His avoidance of friends and refusal to be in circumstances that remind him of the event, however, do not break the cycle. By isolating himself from normal social rhythms and refusing to face the dark, Elias inadvertently keeps the memories fresh and unprocessed. This avoidance feeds directly back into the triggers, making every crowded deck or unfamiliar location feel newly urgent. At the same time, the persistent recurrence of the bodily reenactment and visual fragments warps his view of himself, convincing him that he is fundamentally isolated and set apart from others. His negative appraisal that he belongs nowhere then warps the memories themselves, making the visual fragments sharper and the bodily sensations more inescapable. The persistent recurrence of the bodily reenactment and visual fragments makes him hyper-vigilant, so that familiar physical locations and crowded spaces instantly register as threats. His negative appraisal that he belongs nowhere then amplifies the original triggers; the feeling of isolation makes crowded spaces feel suddenly hostile, and the belief that he is set apart turns familiar physical locations into potential traps. Over months, this loop has tightened into an inescapable architecture. His punishment thinking-the quiet, relentless voice telling him he deserves to suffer-feeds directly back into the triggers, so that familiar physical locations and crowded spaces instantly register as threats. The memory of the flood becomes sharper because his avoidance starves him of corrective experiences, which reinforces the negative appraisal that he no longer belongs anywhere. Elias finally came to therapy seeking help because the punishment thinking has become exhausting, and the belief that he belongs nowhere has begun to fracture his marriage. He is most afraid of sinking back into the water, but he hopes, finally, to stop telling himself he deserves to suffer and to reclaim the man he was before the storm.
